Military Transition Advice: Jacob Mousseau Podcast

Veteran career coach Jacob Mousseau joins Ryan Guina on The Military Wallet Podcast to discuss military transition challenges, veteran job searches, identity loss, burnout, AI tools, and practical advice for life after service.

Published August 25, 2026
Written by Jennifer Barnhill
Published August 25, 2026

Why trust The Military Wallet? We’re a veteran-founded resource that has helped millions make strong financial decisions.

For many servicemembers, the military transition is treated like a checklist: attend TAP class, update a résumé, apply for jobs, move on. But for countless veterans, the reality is far more complicated.

In a recent episode of the Military Wallet Podcast, host Ryan Guina sat down with veteran career coach Jacob Mousseau for a candid conversation about what really happens when military service ends, sometimes unexpectedly.

The discussion moves beyond résumés and interview tips, diving into identity loss, burnout, financial pressure, unhealthy coping mechanisms, and the emotional realities many veterans face after separating from service. At the same time, the episode offers practical advice for veterans trying to navigate an increasingly difficult job market.

When the Military Transition Isn’t Your Choice

Mousseau’s own transition story began with uncertainty.

A ten-year Army veteran, he expected to continue serving after reenlisting during a deployment to Afghanistan. Instead, military downsizing in 2015 abruptly changed the course of his career. His unit at Fort Campbell was selected for inactivation, and within six months, he found himself preparing to leave the Army with little time to build a plan.

That experience mirrors what many veterans encounter. While some leave after a single enlistment, others spend years assuming they will stay until retirement, only to discover that medical issues, force reductions, or family needs can suddenly change those plans.

“One thing we can all do is try planning,” Guina, an Air Force veteran and currently serving member of the National Guard, noted during the conversation. “The day we get in, we know we’re going to leave one day.”

The episode repeatedly returns to a difficult truth: transition is often underestimated, even by military leaders trying to help.

Why Veteran Career Advice Often Falls Short

One of the strongest themes throughout the conversation is the gap between military culture and civilian employment.

Mousseau explained that many transitioning servicemembers receive career advice from leaders who have never made the transition themselves. Well-intentioned guidance can unintentionally create unrealistic expectations about the civilian job market, veteran hiring programs, or how easily military skills transfer into corporate roles.

That disconnect can leave veterans frustrated when they discover civilian industries operate very differently from military organizations.

Mousseau shared his own experience entering human resources after leaving the Army, assuming his leadership background and personnel experience would translate naturally into civilian HR work. Instead, he found an entirely different professional environment with new expectations, policies, and workplace dynamics.

The lesson, he says, is that veterans need to seek advice from people who have already navigated the transition successfully.

Resources like the Department of Defense Transition Assistance Program (TAP), the VA Veteran Readiness and Employment Program (VR&E), and veteran-focused nonprofits can provide support, but Mousseau argues that preparation requires deeper self-reflection than simply attending a class or earning a certification.

The Problem With “I Can Do Anything”

Many veterans leave the military believing their adaptability is their greatest strength. In some ways, it is.

Military members often manage operations, personnel, logistics, administration, and leadership simultaneously. But Mousseau warns that the “Swiss Army knife” mindset can become a liability during civilian hiring.

Employers are usually searching for someone who can solve a specific problem in a specific role.

That means veterans need to narrow their focus.

Throughout the podcast, Mousseau emphasizes the importance of identifying what actually matters before pursuing certifications, degrees, or career changes. Too often, veterans rush into programs like project management certifications or graduate school without first understanding whether those careers align with their values, lifestyle goals, or long-term interests.

He encourages veterans to ask themselves difficult questions:

  • What kind of work energizes you?
  • What kind of work drains you?
  • Is location important?
  • Is work-life balance more valuable than salary?
  • What kind of culture do you want around you?

“Everything can’t be important,” Mousseau reminded listeners during the interview. “Because then nothing’s important.”

Burnout, Identity Loss, and the Emotional Side of Transition

The emotional side of military transition is another major focus of the episode.

Guina openly discusses his own post-service burnout after multiple deployments and years of high operational tempo. Like many veterans, he left the military knowing only that he needed change, but not necessarily understanding what he wanted next.

That uncertainty is common.

Mousseau explains that many veterans spend years bouncing between jobs, searching for purpose while dealing with stress, trauma, financial instability, or strained relationships. Some develop unhealthy coping mechanisms along the way.

The podcast explores how poor transitions can contribute to larger issues like substance abuse, financial hardship, homelessness, divorce, and suicide risk among veterans.

Organizations like AmericaServes, Hiring Our Heroes, and the Veterans Crisis Line offer a variety of resources for veterans struggling during or after transition.

But one of the strongest messages from the conversation is that veterans should not try to navigate transition alone.

“You’ve never done a solo mission in your entire life,” Mousseau says. “Don’t start now.”

How Veterans Can Use AI During a Job Search

The episode also tackles one of the fastest-changing parts of the modern hiring process: artificial intelligence.

Both Guina and Mousseau discuss the growing role AI tools play in career exploration, interview preparation, résumé building, and salary research.

Mousseau uses AI to help veterans identify career paths aligned with their skills, geographic preferences, family needs, and personal values. He also recommends using AI to research companies, practice interview questions, analyze local job markets, and better understand salary expectations.

Still, he cautions against relying on AI blindly.

“Garbage in, garbage out,” Guina says during the discussion, warning that poor prompts often produce inaccurate or misleading results.

Mousseau adds that AI-generated résumés can exaggerate experience or include inaccurate information that may backfire during interviews if candidates cannot speak confidently about what is listed.

Instead, both encourage veterans to treat AI as a research assistant, not a replacement for critical thinking.

For veterans interested in exploring AI tools responsibly, resources like LinkedIn Learning offer introductory guidance on AI-assisted workflows and professional development.

Practical Advice for Veterans Starting Over

Toward the end of the episode, the conversation becomes deeply practical.

Mousseau urges veterans with financial stability to take advantage of the time they have before transitioning. That means networking intentionally, conducting informational interviews, and building a plan instead of “winging it.”

For veterans already struggling financially, his advice is more urgent: stabilize first.

That may mean taking a temporary job, even if it is not the ideal long-term career move.

“Pride and ego get in the way,” he explains. “That’s where families fall apart.”

The message is not about giving up on larger goals. It is about surviving long enough to build toward them.

A Conversation about More than Careers

While the episode is filled with career advice, its larger message is ultimately about identity, purpose, and rebuilding after military service.

Transition is not simply a professional challenge. For many veterans, it is a deeply personal one.

And as both Guina and Mousseau make clear throughout the conversation, a successful transition rarely happens through résumés alone. It requires planning, honesty, support systems, and a willingness to rethink what success looks like after the military.

Veterans interested in learning more can follow Jacob Mousseau on LinkedIn and explore his “Way Home” transition series on YouTube through Frontline Career Strategy.
